content: The World Health Organization (WHO) convened its second consultation on translating tuberculosis (TB) research into global policy guidelines on March 15–16, 2022. This meeting aimed to review progress, identify emerging needs, and provide updated guidance to achieve the goals of the WHO End TB Strategy. The consultation brought together scientists, public health experts, civil society representatives, and country stakeholders to discuss TB prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care. Key Highlights from the Consultation: 1. Screening and Prevention WHO presented its latest consolidated guidance on TB preventive treatment (TPT), infection prevention and control (IPC), and TB screening, along with operational handbooks. Updates to the IPC guidelines and new developments in biomarkers and digital adherence technologies were also shared. Discussions emphasized the need for further research to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of new screening approaches and improve the sensitivity and specificity of symptom-based screening, particularly for high-risk groups other than people living with HIV. For TPT, ongoing trials (e.g., VQUIN and TB CHAMP) on drug-resistant TB contacts were highlighted. If results are favorable, countries will require support to scale up interventions rapidly, including guidance on service delivery. For pediatric populations, updating recommendations on short-course TPT regimens (e.g., 3HP and 1HP) remains a priority, especially with the anticipated availability of child-friendly formulations like water-dispersible rifapentine. 2. Diagnostics WHO shared updates on TB diagnostics, including the 2021 policy on nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) and the 2022 policy on alternative interferon-gamma release assays for TB infection diagnosis. The first WHO catalog of Mycobacterium tuberculosis mutations and updates to target product profiles for drug susceptibility testing (DST) were also presented. The shift to class-based recommendations for diagnostics aims to enhance market competition and provide countries with more options suited to their contexts. Emerging areas of focus include diagnostics for subclinical TB and non-sputum-based tests, particularly for children. The lack of validated biomarkers in non-sputum samples remains a challenge. 3. Treatment Updates on WHO guidelines for drug-susceptible TB (DS-TB) and drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) treatment were presented, including the evolution of shorter, all-oral regimens. The ongoing development of a global individual patient data platform for DR-TB treatment was also discussed. Reducing drug toxicity and optimizing shorter regimens for DR-TB remain priorities. The role of new drugs like pretomanid and delamanid in universal TB regimens is being explored. Participants emphasized the need for equitable access to DST before introducing new drugs and highlighted the importance of person-centered care approaches, including social, psychological, and economic support for patients. 4. Child and Adolescent TB The burden of TB among children and adolescents was discussed, with a focus on challenges in case detection and access to TPT. The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on pediatric TB was also highlighted. WHO’s updated guidance on managing TB in children and adolescents includes new recommendations and operational handbooks. Ongoing studies are expected to inform future policy updates. Key priorities include defining non-severe TB in children, scaling up access to chest radiography, and addressing the lack of age-appropriate formulations for DR-TB treatment. 5. TB Comorbidities and Vulnerable Populations WHO outlined priority drivers of TB and risk factors for poor treatment outcomes, including HIV, diabetes, malnutrition, smoking, and mental health disorders. Despite existing guidelines, countries have been slow to scale up action on TB comorbidities, except for HIV-associated TB. A new Framework for Collaborative Action on TB and Comorbidities is being developed to strengthen cross-sectoral collaboration and deliver person-centered care. Participants stressed the importance of including individuals with comorbidities in TB research and developing standardized study protocols to address evidence gaps. 6. Social Protection and Disability Achieving End TB targets requires addressing the social and economic determinants of TB. WHO presented its approach to social protection and patient support, including plans to repackage existing recommendations into a TB social protection guidance document. Research gaps on TB-associated disability and social protection were discussed, with participants emphasizing the need for evidence-based policies to address these challenges. Conclusion: The consultation underscored the importance of evidence-based policies, equitable access to care, and person-centered approaches to TB prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. WHO will continue to consolidate and update its guidelines to address emerging needs and support countries in achieving the End TB Strategy targets.
